n: The book closes with a census that brings judgment. Here the Lord is said to “move” David; the parallel account in 1 Chronicles says Satan provoked him. Scripture often describes God as the ultimate cause of what He permits.

f.g: Take a census, likely for military conscription or taxation.

n: David orders Joab to count all the fighting men from Dan in the north to Beer-sheba in the south. His motive seems to be pride in his own strength rather than trust in God.

f.g: The whole country, north to south.

f.w: that I may know the number of the people

n: Even Joab objects: may God multiply Israel a hundred times — but why does the king want to count them? He senses this is wrong.

f.w: why doth my lord the king delight in this thing?

n: The king overrules Joab and the army officers, and they set out to take the census.

f.g: Overruled.

n: The census-takers begin east of the Jordan, at Aroer by the Arnon gorge in the south, and move north toward Jazer.

f.g: A town on the Arnon River, Israel’s southern border east of the Jordan.

n: They continue through Gilead and up to Dan and the region near Sidon in the far north.

f.g: An unknown place; the text may be damaged here.
Sidon, a Phoenician city on the coast.

n: They go to the fortress of Tyre and the Canaanite and Hivite cities, then south through Judah to Beer-sheba.

f.g: One of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel.

n: The census takes nearly ten months to complete.
Joab reports 800,000 fighting men in Israel and 500,000 in Judah. (1 Chronicles 21:5 gives different figures, perhaps counting differently.)
Afterward David’s conscience strikes him. He confesses that he has sinned greatly and acted foolishly, and he asks God to take away his guilt. His quick, honest repentance is a mark of his character.

f.g: His conscience troubled him.

n: The next morning, the Lord gives a message to Gad, David’s prophet.

f.g: A prophet who sees by revelation.

n: God offers David a choice of three consequences.
The choices: years of famine, three months fleeing from enemies, or three days of plague. David must decide what answer to send back.

f.g: 1 Chronicles 21:12 reads “three years,” which matches the pattern of three.
A deadly epidemic or plague.

n: David chooses to fall into the hands of the Lord, trusting His great mercy, rather than the hands of men. Even in judgment, he knows God is more merciful than people.

f.g: A terrible dilemma; great distress.

n: The plague strikes, and seventy thousand people die across the land. The king’s sin affects the whole nation.

f.g: The appointed end of the three days; or perhaps the time of the evening sacrifice.

n: As the destroying angel reaches out over Jerusalem, the Lord relents and stops him. The angel stands by the threshing floor of Araunah — a location that will become sacred.

f.w: the LORD repented him of the evil
f.g: The Lord relented from the calamity — He chose mercy. “Evil” here means disaster, not sin.
Called Ornan in 1 Chronicles 21:15; a Jebusite who owned land in Jerusalem.

n: Seeing the angel, David pleads for his people: he is the one who sinned; what have these sheep done? Let the punishment fall on him and his family. Like a true shepherd, he offers himself for the flock.

f.w: these sheep, what have they done?

n: Gad tells David to build an altar on Araunah’s threshing floor.
David obeys the Lord’s command through the prophet.
Araunah sees the king coming and bows to the ground before him.
David explains he has come to buy the threshing floor to build an altar so the plague will stop.

f.g: Stayed = stopped.

n: Araunah generously offers everything for free: the floor, oxen for sacrifice, and the wooden threshing sledges and yokes for firewood.

f.g: Heavy wooden sledges dragged over grain to thresh it.

n: Araunah gives like a king and prays that God will accept David’s offering.

f.g: Generously, royally; or possibly “O king.”

n: David refuses: he will not offer to God something that costs him nothing. True sacrifice must cost the giver. He pays fifty shekels of silver.

f.w: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing

f.g: Chronicles says 600 shekels of gold, perhaps for the whole site.

n: David builds the altar and offers sacrifices, and the Lord hears the prayer for the land; the plague stops. This very site would become the place where Solomon built the temple — on Mount Moriah, where Abraham once offered Isaac. Sacrifice and mercy meet there, pointing to the atoning sacrifice of Christ.

f.w: David built there an altar unto the LORD

f.g: The Lord responded to prayer.
